To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) the myofilament activation response to a stretch is not a simple linear response, but is instead a highly complex and non-linear one; (b) the myofilaments are not uniformly stretched during a stretch, but instead experience localized strains that differ from the overall strain; and (c) these localized strains can be modeled as a function of sarcomere length and the amount of stretch.
The Frank–Starling law of the heart, a key component of the normal cardiovascular system, has a mechanistic basis in myofilament strain.

the Frank–Startling relationship is probably a complex integration of multiple mechanisms that involve the entire myocyte and that the best way to understand the mechanisms involved is to develop a computational model of the myocyte that can be used to explore the effects of changes in each of these mechanisms.

The main takeaway from our work is that
myocyte strain can have a significant effect on myofilament activation by modulating the Ca2+ affinity of troponin C and/or the cooperativity of the thin filament.
the Frank-Starling relationship is probably not a single process.
myofibrillars are complex structures that are capable of sensing and responding to local strain.
